Yes, I understand what you mean. You're not intervening too much: this is the right starting point, and I've moved it ahead of the G-optimisation work.

**What the exploration covers.** Take a fixed G and read it with windows of width ω = 1, 2, 3, … At each width, list which numbers it generates, check whether G is "ω-complete" (it generates every number in [0, 2^ω)), and draw it. Each sequence gets one row per ω, showing which of the 2^ω numbers it hits.

**Two structural facts that organise it:**
- **Completeness only goes downward.** If G is 5-complete it is automatically 4-, 3-, 2- and 1-complete, because every shorter word is the start of some longer one. So your "mix" of complete widths collapses to a single number per sequence, its completeness order c(G). The richer part is above that order: what fraction of the 2^ω numbers it still reaches at each width, and which numbers are missing.
- **Widening the window is a dynamical system.** Going from width ω to ω+1 doubles each number and appends one bit, which is the map x ↦ 2x mod 1. ω-completeness then means the sequence visits every interval [j/2^ω, (j+1)/2^ω). Sequences complete at every width are already a studied class (disjunctive and normal sequences, e.g. Champernowne's). That is a good sign the space really does obey laws, as you suspected.

**What the agent will measure:**
- exact counts over every G up to about length 20;
- sampled random G at larger lengths, to find where completeness switches on and how sharply;
- named families: de Bruijn, LFSR, Thue–Morse, Fibonacci, Champernowne, periodic and random sequences.

**Wave 1.** The literature map is in [00-findings_v0.md](__reports__/literature/00-findings_v0.md). Its main result is that the fixed-stride and mapped-read versions of your idea already exist in recent LLM weight compression (QTIP, building on Mao & Gray 2010). Something close to the literal pointer version also exists: SeedLM stores a seed per block of weights. The combinatorics we're now exploring is not covered by either. The foundations theory agent is still running.

The two optimisation nodes (superstring G and trellis) are on hold until the exploration reports. I'll re-plan them from what it finds.

Wave 1 is finished. The foundations report is [00-findings_v0.md](__reports__/foundations/00-findings_v0.md); I re-checked its main theorems myself before closing the node.

**What is now proved:**
- **Your literal scheme only pays off on redundant data.** For a fixed G, the fraction of targets it can encode is exactly (p_G(ω)/2^ω)^m. Pointers save bits only when the number of window positions n−ω+1 is at most 2^(ω−1), which means G covers at most half of all ω-bit numbers.
- **A fully universal G gives zero gain.** If G can produce every number at width ω, a de Bruijn sequence is optimal, but each pointer still costs at least ω bits. Whatever you save is bounded by how redundant the data is.
- **Several G's or variable-length reads don't change this.**
- **The fixed-stride version reaches the counting bound exactly.** Its output map is one-to-one whenever the stride is at most ω, so it is as efficient as counting allows.
- **Coverage of a random G is well predicted.** The simple formula 2^ω(1 − e^(−(n−ω+1)/2^ω)) is off by at most 0.37 words, for ω up to 14.
- **A random G becomes complete late.** It needs about (ω+1)·ln 2 times the de Bruijn length to cover every ω-bit number.

**The first unexplained law.** Count the sequences G that produce exactly p distinct ω-bit numbers. That count is 2, 6, 20, 58, 164, 430, 1112, 2770, 6782, 16270, …, and it is the same for every length n and window ω as long as p ≤ min(ω, n−ω). I confirmed it by brute force on four (n, ω) pairs. **Laws I verified by brute force:**
- **Completeness switches on sharply for random G.** The chance of being ω-complete jumps from near 0 to near 1 around n ≈ 2^ω(ω·ln2 + 0.37), and that jump gets relatively narrower as ω grows. The all-zeros and all-ones windows are always the last to appear.
- **Low-complexity sequences have an explicit structure.** The count 2, 6, 20, 58, … comes from a periodic core with a few free bits at each end. The formula matches every count through p = 10.
- **Complete sequences just above the minimum length are countable.** At length 2^ω + ω there are 2^(2^(ω−1))·(11/2 − 2^(2−ω)) of them; I confirmed this for ω = 2, 3, 4. It is still a conjecture.
- **Champernowne is slow to complete.** It is the classic normal sequence, yet it becomes ω-complete only after exactly (ω−1)·2^ω + ω + 2 bits. That is slower than a random sequence, because the all-zeros word first appears inside the number 2^ω. I confirmed this for ω = 2 to 8.
- **Composition never compresses uniform data.** Building numbers from several reads costs, on average, at least about 1.4 times the number's own bit length in every sequence family tested.

**A law that appears only in the figure:**
- Low-entropy sequences (periodic, Fibonacci, Thue–Morse) generate a Cantor-like dust of numbers.
- Random and normal sequences fill the whole range until the sequence runs out of length.
- I expect the "dimension" of that dust to equal the entropy rate of G, which is also the best compression rate G can give. If that holds, your generative space and the compression question are one theory.

**Wave 3 is now running as four agents:**
- **Proofs:** the atlas agent is proving the low-complexity formula and the entropy–dimension law; a second agent will then try to break those proofs.
- **Your literal scheme on real data:** G is built per target as a shortest string containing every distinct block, plus one pointer per block. It runs on an image and on MiniLM and Gemma weights, against block entropy and zlib/lzma.
- **Fixed-stride windows:** reading the windows raw versus mapping them to values first (the gap the literature leaves), compared against the theoretical best.

**The answer to your question.** Your G, now called the **imbrex**, is a rich combinatorial object and a poor compressor.

**The generative space has clean laws.** These are proofs that a separate agent tried to break and couldn't:
- **Single-window completeness only goes downward**, so each imbrex has a completeness order c(G). Composed reads (your 5+3 example) reach every 8-bit number exactly when c(G) ≥ 5.
- **Minimal complete imbrices** are de Bruijn words, and there are 2^(2^(ω−1)) of them. At one bit longer the count is exactly 2^(2^(ω−1)−ω)(11·2^(ω−1)−4).
- **The count 2, 6, 20, 58, … of very poor imbrices** does not depend on length or window width. It is explained by an explicit structure: a periodic core plus a few free bits at each end.
- **Entropy equals dimension.** Low-entropy imbrices generate a Cantor-like dust of numbers; that was your reading of the barcode figure, and it is now a theorem.
- **Random imbrices switch to complete sharply**, around n ≈ 2^ω(ω ln 2 + 0.37). Champernowne's normal sequence is slower than random.

**Compression is governed by something else.** It depends on how often each window gets used, not on which numbers the imbrex can produce.
- Counting caps any saving at the redundancy of the data.
- Your literal scheme (imbrex plus pointers) never beat lzma on a real image or on MiniLM/Gemma weights.
- If the pointers are entropy-coded, every imbrex gives the same rate, so the imbrex only adds its own length as overhead.
- Fixed-stride raw reading is exactly a repetition code, so a wider window never helps.
- The version that does work is QTIP-style trellis quantization, which passes each window through a scrambling map; with a random map it comes within 0.38 dB of the theoretical bound.

**Your idea already exists in the literature, in parts:**
- SeedLM uses a universal imbrex with a seed per block as the pointer.
- Mao & Gray (2010) and QTIP (2024) use the fixed-stride reading with a map.
- Piṅgala's *yamātārājabhānasalagām* is the oldest recorded minimal complete imbrex.

The combinatorics of what an imbrex generates is the part I didn't find covered anywhere.

**Two things to know:**
- **One favourable number is not measured.** A rate of about 0.89 on weights, against about 0.92 for lzma, comes from a formula for an adaptive pointer coder that was never built. The notebook labels it as an estimate. I've proposed a follow-up session (card above) to build the coder and settle it.
- **Some checks were weak.** References that agents cited from memory are flagged as unverified, and the web check that "imbrex" isn't already a term in coding or combinatorics was only partial.

**The generative space has clean laws.** These are proofs that a separate agent tried to break and couldn't:
- **Single-window completeness only goes downward**, so each imbrex has a completeness order c(G). Composed reads (your 5+3 example) reach every 8-bit number exactly when c(G) ≥ 5.
- **Minimal complete imbrices** are de Bruijn words, and there are 2^(2^(ω−1)) of them. At one bit longer the count is exactly 2^(2^(ω−1)−ω)(11·2^(ω−1)−4).
- **The count 2, 6, 20, 58, … of very poor imbrices** does not depend on length or window width. It is explained by an explicit structure: a periodic core plus a few free bits at each end.
- **Entropy equals dimension.** Low-entropy imbrices generate a Cantor-like dust of numbers; that was your reading of the barcode figure, and it is now a theorem.
- **Random imbrices switch to complete sharply**, around n ≈ 2^ω(ω ln 2 + 0.37). Champernowne's normal sequence is slower than random.

My take is that the gap was never in the theory. What happened in 2024 is that an old theory finally became worth engineering, because the constraints changed. Your cold-storage case is a different problem from the one QTIP solves, and the study already answers most of it.

**Why something like QTIP appears only in 2024**
- **The limits are old.** Shannon's rate–distortion bound dates from 1959. Trellis quantization reached within about 0.4 dB of it by around 1990, and the bit-shift trellis that QTIP builds on is Mao & Gray, 2010. QTIP did not discover new room.
- **Two constraints changed:**
  - Decoding now has to run on GPUs, massively in parallel, fast enough to keep up with memory bandwidth, for hundreds of billions of numbers. Classical trellis coding never had to decode like that. QTIP's contribution is making the old trellis cheap to decode on that hardware.
  - Its target was runtime VRAM, which is exactly the use you set aside.
- **A prerequisite only arrived in 2023.** Random rotations of the weights (QuIP's "incoherence processing") make weights look Gaussian. Only then does a Gaussian-optimal quantizer apply.
- **Scale made the margins worth it.** When serving costs are measured in GPU fleets, 0.1 bit per weight is worth real money. The "pockets" you see are mostly old theory meeting a new constraint, not unexplored mathematics.

**Your actual use: cold storage of exact models**

That is lossless compression, and here the study's main result applies directly: the saving is capped by the redundancy of the data.
- **Per weight, the redundancy is small and its location is known.** Sign and mantissa bits of trained weights are close to random. Nearly all the redundancy sits in the exponent bits, which carry about 2–3 bits of information instead of 8. This matches our measurement: lzma got only about 8% on float32 slices.
- **Dedicated tools already reach the limit.** ZipNN (2024) and DFloat11 (2025) entropy-code the exponents and get BF16 models to roughly 66–70% of their size, losslessly. These figures are from memory; I did not verify them in this study. So there is no hidden pocket left in a single model file.
- **The real win for a drive full of models is across models.** Most local collections are a base model plus fine-tunes, merges or variants of it. A fine-tune differs only slightly from its base, so storing the base once and each variant as an entropy-coded difference (an XOR of the bits, or a delta) can shrink variants dramatically. This is your imbrex idea in its useful form:
  - the base model is the shared G;
  - each variant is described relative to it.

  It is the lossless version of the "shared imbrex for a model family" open problem, and it is where the redundancy actually is.
- **If you can accept loss, the gain is much larger.** A 4-bit quantized copy (GGUF-style) is about a quarter of BF16 and usually fine for testing. Storing that instead of the original is where QTIP-class methods pay off.

So for your SSD: entropy-code the exponents (about 30% off each file), store fine-tunes as deltas against their base (often most of their size), and keep 4-bit copies for anything you only test. If you want, I can measure the delta approach on two related models you have locally.

Your intuition is right, and the degradation is not unmeasurable. The quantity has a name: the conditional entropy H(B | A), the bits needed to describe checkpoint B once you already have A. Your "continuity between checkpoints" is the mutual information between them, and how well a shared base pays off is roughly I(A;B)/H(B).

**How it degrades for neural-net checkpoints (same architecture)**
- **Delta cost grows with the logarithm of the update size.** Take the XOR of two float bit patterns. If a weight moved by a relative amount ε, the sign, the exponent and the top ~log₂(1/ε) mantissa bits stay identical, and only the low bits differ. So the cost per weight is roughly the mantissa width minus log₂(1/ε), or zero when the change doesn't survive rounding, which happens often in bf16.
- **That gives a cheap proxy**: the per-tensor relative norm ‖Δw‖/‖w‖.
- **Consecutive pretraining checkpoints follow the learning-rate schedule.** Early checkpoints have large updates and almost no saving. Late ones, after the learning rate has decayed, have small updates and good savings.
- **Fine-tunes usually sit close to their base.** For LoRA-style fine-tunes, storing the adapter itself beats any generic diff. Knowing how the change was made always beats blind diffing.

**Where continuity breaks completely**
- **Architecture changes**, such as a new tokenizer, different widths or re-initialised layers, leave no coordinate correspondence to diff against.
- **Retraining the same architecture from a different seed** is the subtle case. A network's neurons can be permuted without changing what it computes, so two independently trained models can be functionally similar while their raw weights look unrelated. You must align them before diffing (permutation alignment, as in "Git Re-Basin", 2022).

**The genetics and git analogy**
- **Genomics is the cleanest success of your idea.** A reference genome is stored once, and each individual becomes a list of variants against it, as in VCF files or CRAM reference-based compression. Three gigabytes shrink to megabytes because two humans are about 99.9% identical. The reference is literally a shared imbrex, and each person is pointers plus mutations. The study's regime A failed on uniform data because it had no such reference. The idea works when the reference carries most of the information.
- **The genomics workflow also shows the missing step for models: alignment before diffing.** Sequences get aligned before mutations are called. Models need neuron alignment before deltas mean anything.
- **Git's deltas are regime A with variable-length reads.** Packfiles store "copy bytes i..j from the base" plus inserted literals, which is relative Lempel–Ziv (RLZ), one of the works the literature map found. Git also does not always diff against the parent; it picks whichever stored object makes the smallest delta.
- **With many versions, choosing the bases becomes a tree problem.** You get a weighted graph whose edge costs are delta sizes, and you want the cheapest spanning arborescence (Edmonds' algorithm). That is a phylogenetic tree in compression terms, e.g. base → instruct → domain fine-tunes.

So the efficiency of a shared imbrex is not a mysterious function of "architecture and training changes". It is H(B | A), it can be estimated per tensor from ‖Δw‖/‖w‖, and it collapses only where the coordinates stop corresponding.

**Checkpoints within one training run are where the law predicts big savings.** These numbers come from the slope we measured, not from a measurement:
- **Step size:** between consecutive checkpoints of one run, each weight typically moves by about 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻² of its size, depending on the learning rate at that point and how many steps separate the two saves. Gemma's instruct model moved 6%.
- **Mid-training:** at about 1 bit saved per halving of the update, a checkpoint coded against the previous one should keep roughly 4–9 more shared high bits per weight than Gemma's pair. That is plausibly 2–4× smaller, losslessly.
- **Late training:** the learning rate has decayed and the gain is largest.
- **Early training:** large updates, close to nothing.
- **Precision:** checkpoints usually keep FP32 master weights, which have more low bits to share.
- **Optimizer state:** a training checkpoint also stores the Adam moments, typically two FP32 copies the size of the model, so it is several times larger than the model. Those moments change more erratically from save to save, which caps the overall gain.

**Is the community already doing it? Partly.** I'm citing these from memory and haven't verified them this session:
- **Lossy checkpoint compression** is an active line of work. Examples: Check-N-Run (Meta, 2022, recommendation models); LC-Checkpoint and Delta-DNN (around 2020); ExCP (2024), which compresses LLM checkpoint weights and optimizer momentum together by large factors on Pythia. They store pruned and quantized residuals between checkpoints, so they give up exactness.
- **Lossy fine-tune deltas:** BitDelta and DeltaZip (2024) compress the fine-tune minus base difference to 1–2 bits per weight to serve many variants. That is again lossy.
- **Byte-level deduplication:** Hugging Face's Xet storage (your cache has an `xet` folder) splits files into chunks by content and stores identical chunks once. It catches unchanged tensors and re-uploads, but not fine-tunes, since we measured only ~3% of weights to be bit-identical.
- **Lossless numeric deltas between checkpoints** of the kind we just measured (integer differences of ordered float bits, entropy-coded) are the least crowded part as far as I know. In practice people mostly keep fewer checkpoints rather than compress them.

Good question, and it can be tested directly rather than argued. "Aligning the bit sequences themselves", the way genomes are aligned, means finding long identical stretches of bits that occur in both files and pointing to them instead of storing them. `zstd --patch-from` does exactly that: it searches the whole reference file for the longest matches, as relative Lempel–Ziv does. I tested it directly: aligning the raw bit sequences, the way genomes are aligned, saves **exactly nothing** on all three pairs. That includes the late Pythia checkpoints, where comparing each weight with its counterpart saved 23%. Details are in [04-findings_v4.md](__reports__/reference_coding/04-findings_v4.md).

**Why genome-style alignment finds nothing.** Two versions of a model are already perfectly aligned: same tensors, same order, same positions, no insertions or deletions. What differs is that *every* number changed slightly. In genome terms, every single letter carries a small mutation, so no long identical stretch survives anywhere. Alignment looks for identical stretches and finds only chance matches about one float long. What the two versions share sits at the same position: the high-order bits of each weight. Comparing position by position captures that, which is why the numeric difference works and alignment doesn't.

**On "the larger the reference, the more overlap".** The earlier research says the opposite for compression, and it's one of the few things it proves:
- **Expressivity grows with size.** In a reference of n bits, the longest match for a random target grows like log₂ n. That is atlas law L14: log₂ n + 0.3 for random sequences.
- **But using a match costs a pointer of log₂ n bits.** The match lengthens and the pointer lengthens at the same rate, so for data that shares nothing beyond chance the net saving stays zero.

That is the counting bound seen from the alignment side. A larger imbrex lets you *express* more, but it never makes chance overlap free. Only overlap caused by shared history pays: a common base, adjacent checkpoints.

**Your "function of the first" does exist, in its extreme form.** BERT seed 1 is a tiny function of seed 0: "rerun the same training with seed 1", a few kilobytes of code plus a number. The two models do share information, but only through the training process, not through their coordinates. Decoding that function costs a full training run, and GPU nondeterminism means it wouldn't reproduce the stored bits exactly.

**1. ω, not k.** Agreed: ω is the window over each weight's bits, so I'll use ω from here on. The format question can be tested by simulation. Quantize the same Pythia pair into several storage formats and measure, per format, what the reference saves:
- BF16 and FP8-E4M3;

One limitation upfront: Pythia's checkpoints hold FP16 values, so true FP32 training precision can't be measured from them. The ω* law predicts what it would show.

**2. Rotation: you're right, and I was wrong.** I said a rotation "would change the stored floats". That only matters if you store the rotated weights. You don't: you use the rotated seed-0 model as a *predictor* and store seed 1's exact difference from that prediction. The decoder recomputes the prediction, so this stays lossless. The rotation can be computed, mostly in closed form:
- **Residual stream:** an orthogonal Procrustes fit, solved by one SVD, on the token embeddings, which are shared token by token.

**The answer to your question.** Your G, now called the **imbrex**, is a rich combinatorial object and a poor compressor.

**The generative space has clean laws.** These are proofs that a separate agent tried to break and couldn't:
- **Single-window completeness only goes downward**, so each imbrex has a completeness order c(G). Composed reads (your 5+3 example) reach every 8-bit number exactly when c(G) ≥ 5.
- **Minimal complete imbrices** are de Bruijn words, and there are 2^(2^(ω−1)) of them. At one bit longer the count is exactly 2^(2^(ω−1)−ω)(11·2^(ω−1)−4).
- **The count 2, 6, 20, 58, … of very poor imbrices** does not depend on length or window width. It is explained by an explicit structure: a periodic core plus a few free bits at each end.
- **Entropy equals dimension.** Low-entropy imbrices generate a Cantor-like dust of numbers; that was your reading of the barcode figure, and it is now a theorem.
- **Random imbrices switch to complete sharply**, around n ≈ 2^ω(ω ln 2 + 0.37). Champernowne's normal sequence is slower than random.

**Compression is governed by something else.** It depends on how often each window gets used, not on which numbers the imbrex can produce.
- Counting caps any saving at the redundancy of the data.
- Your literal scheme (imbrex plus pointers) never beat lzma on a real image or on MiniLM/Gemma weights.
- If the pointers are entropy-coded, every imbrex gives the same rate, so the imbrex only adds its own length as overhead.
- Fixed-stride raw reading is exactly a repetition code, so a wider window never helps.
- The version that does work is QTIP-style trellis quantization, which passes each window through a scrambling map; with a random map it comes within 0.38 dB of the theoretical bound.

**Your idea already exists in the literature, in parts:**
- SeedLM uses a universal imbrex with a seed per block as the pointer.
- Mao & Gray (2010) and QTIP (2024) use the fixed-stride reading with a map.
- Piṅgala's *yamātārājabhānasalagām* is the oldest recorded minimal complete imbrex.

Yes, I think that's the right axis. Here is how this session sits on it.

**The two modes want different things from the PI.**

| | Exploration (attention) | Hardening (mechanics) |
|:--|:--|:--|
| What drives it | a hunch, something that doesn't add up, taste | a stated claim |
| Its only real limit | budget | correctness |
| Is "most promising" debatable? | always; experts disagree | rarely; the claim is either supported or not |
| What helps | raw material, freedom, room to be wrong | rules, labels, reproduction, proofs, statistical power |
| Who should do it | the PI itself, or one agent with a loose brief | agents with tight briefs, plus independent checkers |

**This session's split, roughly, by agent tokens:**
- Exploration got about a quarter (literature and the atlas, ~600k).
- Hardening got about half (foundations, laws, both experiments, reproduction, proof review, ~1.3M).
- Synthesis got the last quarter (notebook, naming).

The hardening side was well run; that's where the rules belonged, and they caught real errors. The atlas, the one loosely briefed exploratory wave, came at your prompting, and per token it produced most of what we learned about the object. After wave 3, nothing was left in the budget for the signals that hardening had turned up.

**Most of the balance problem sits at the boundary between the modes.**
- *Exploration to hardening:* when a hunch is worth turning into a claim. That is a judgement call. Once made, the mechanical machinery takes over, and it should.
- *Hardening to exploration:* mechanical work keeps producing anomalies as a by-product, like Bernoulli having h = 1 or a trained map barely beating a random one. That flow is what broke here. I compressed the hardening output into labelled summaries before it reached my attention, so the by-products were filtered out exactly where the next branches would have come from.

**On "most promising" being debatable,** labs hedge with a portfolio: a few cheap probes on several hunches rather than one bet on the "best" branch. With a budget as the only constraint, that fits better than ranking. Applied here, that would have meant three small probes after wave 3: a frequency-weighted generative space, the overlap structure as the asset, and lossy overlapping codebooks. That would have replaced one notebook built on a closed story.

If useful, I can fold this two-mode framing into the knowledge-transfer report as a closing section, with the token split, so the whole retrospective is organised around it rather than around the earlier list of fixes.

**What to reuse from umbod (contracts, not the CLI):**
- **Honesty tags and the uncertainty section.** Its `[source:]`/`[assumption:]` tags and closing "What I am uncertain about" section merge with our claim labels and puzzles. That section *is* the puzzles entry.
- **Its human-facing files.** INTENT is written only by the human, so revising it is a signal; your words in the framing doc become exactly that. INBOX (human appends, agent acknowledges) becomes `/lab-steer`. Soft and hard QUESTIONS replace my ad hoc read-backs.
- **Sealed cycle files.** These give sealed wave notes: the resume anchor, and the record of why each wave ran.
- **Its "senior reviewer judging by feel".** This is a judgement verifier, not a mechanical one. It fits as a depth reviewer before synthesis, distinct from the reproducer and the proof adversary.
- **Who-writes-what.** Its role-asymmetry table and per-agent commit identity carry over.

For campaigns spanning several sessions, umbod stays the outer loop and one cycle holds one or more lab waves. It also already owns `__threads__/`, so our peer-conversation store needs another name; the naming agents know.

**What one entry contains.** Each store is an append-only log of events:
- **ledger:** one row per agent run.
- **lab:** one wave note, sealed when the wave ends.
- **claims:** claim and verdict events.
- **threads:** one message per exchange.
- **puzzles:** raise, follow and park events.

Nothing is updated in place. The current label, the disputed flag, whether a puzzle was followed, and the remaining budget are all computed from the events, so concurrent writers can never lose an update.

**File stores or databases:** both, in different roles.
- The source of truth is **per-writer segment files**, `<store>/<wave>/<agent_id>.jsonl`. Each agent appends only to its own file, so parallel writing needs no locks. Each segment is plain text and diffable, and because no two writers share a file, git never sees a conflict.
- A **derived SQLite index**, gitignored and updated incrementally from byte offsets, serves queries in milliseconds and can be rebuilt by replaying the segments.
- SQLite alone would be binary and unmergeable in git. A shared JSONL file depends on append atomicity, which breaks with large lines or network filesystems. A database server is out of proportion for thousands of rows.

**The utility: one Rust binary with three front ends.**
- A CLI for agents and the human: `append`, `query`, `steer`, `ask`.
- Hook subcommands: `brief`, the ledger, the presence gate, and the guard.
- An MCP stdio server, so agents call typed tools instead of building shell commands.

**Why Rust:** I agree with you. The hooks fire on every tool call of every agent, over 1,000 in this study alone.
- A Rust binary starts in about 1 ms with about 2 MB of memory; Python takes about 30–60 ms and 15–25 MB.
- It has no interpreter or packages to drift, and it matches `dirtree-rdm` and `umbod`.
- The cost is cross-platform builds, which should happen in CI from day one: `dirtree-rdm` still ships darwin-only.

**Sustainability, measured in the ledger rather than preached:**
- **Communication:** briefs reference files instead of pasting them; colgrep retrieval instead of whole-file reads; pairs talk directly instead of through the PI; queries return pointers.
- **Prompt cache:** shared prefixes stay byte-stable, so cache reads are counted.
- **Compute:** model tiering, smallest instance first, and Wolfram for exact work. Reproduction becomes *sampled*: the quick mode plus a random sample of cells, with a full rerun only on a mismatch. This study reran two full sweeps, about double the CPU.
- **Electricity:** an estimated Wh per run, from tokens × a per-model coefficient plus CPU seconds × machine power. It is labelled as an estimate and used to compare runs. Budgets can be stated in Wh as well as tokens.
- **Materials:** no re-downloads; figures referenced or stored as vector graphics rather than embedded. This study's notebook was 14 MB from three embedded PNGs.
- **Human attention:** soft questions are batched, and the brief shows puzzles first.

Once the naming reports are in, I'll pick a coherent set of names and fold everything into architecture v2.

The classical set is in, and it's coherent: one Latin root system built on weighing (*pendere*, *libra*), where paying and judging are the same act. Two names stand out:
- **scrupuli** for puzzles: the sharp pebble in your sandal, and also the smallest weight, a residue that isn't rounded away.
- **libripens** for the tool: the neutral scale-holder in a Roman sale. It is unclaimed as a command name.

Its weak spots: `pondus` already exists as a package name, and `examen` reads as "exam" in Spanish and French. I'll compare it with the transmission-traditions set when that agent reports, then pick.

- **lab:** one wave note, sealed when the wave ends.
- **claims:** claim and verdict events.
- **threads:** one message per exchange.
- **puzzles:** raise, follow and park events.

Nothing is updated in place. The current label, the disputed flag, whether a puzzle was followed, and the remaining budget are all computed from the events, so concurrent writers can never lose an update.

**File stores or databases:** both, in different roles.
- The source of truth is **per-writer segment files**, `<store>/<wave>/<agent_id>.jsonl`. Each agent appends only to its own file, so parallel writing needs no locks. Each segment is plain text and diffable, and because no two writers share a file, git never sees a conflict.
- A **derived SQLite index**, gitignored and updated incrementally from byte offsets, serves queries in milliseconds and can be rebuilt by replaying the segments.
- SQLite alone would be binary and unmergeable in git. A shared JSONL file depends on append atomicity, which breaks with large lines or network filesystems. A database server is out of proportion for thousands of rows.

**The utility: one Rust binary with three front ends.**
- A CLI for agents and the human: `append`, `query`, `steer`, `ask`.
- Hook subcommands: `brief`, the ledger, the presence gate, and the guard.
- An MCP stdio server, so agents call typed tools instead of building shell commands.

**Why Rust:** I agree with you. The hooks fire on every tool call of every agent, over 1,000 in this study alone.
- A Rust binary starts in about 1 ms with about 2 MB of memory; Python takes about 30–60 ms and 15–25 MB.
- It has no interpreter or packages to drift, and it matches `dirtree-rdm` and `umbod`.
- The cost is cross-platform builds, which should happen in CI from day one: `dirtree-rdm` still ships darwin-only.

**Sustainability, measured in the ledger rather than preached:**
- **Communication:** briefs reference files instead of pasting them; colgrep retrieval instead of whole-file reads; pairs talk directly instead of through the PI; queries return pointers.
- **Prompt cache:** shared prefixes stay byte-stable, so cache reads are counted.
- **Compute:** model tiering, smallest instance first, and Wolfram for exact work. Reproduction becomes *sampled*: the quick mode plus a random sample of cells, with a full rerun only on a mismatch. This study reran two full sweeps, about double the CPU.
- **Electricity:** an estimated Wh per run, from tokens × a per-model coefficient plus CPU seconds × machine power. It is labelled as an estimate and used to compare runs. Budgets can be stated in Wh as well as tokens.
- **Materials:** no re-downloads; figures referenced or stored as vector graphics rather than embedded. This study's notebook was 14 MB from three embedded PNGs.
- **Human attention:** soft questions are batched, and the brief shows puzzles first.

Yes, and it fits the design well. Most of it can be measured cheaply and locally, and it gives the human a way to see the problem space instead of reading transcripts. Here is how I'd make it concrete, with the guard I think it needs.

**1. Communication cost in bits, not tokens.** Token counts measure length, not information.
- **Description length of a message:** its compressed size, using zstd with a dictionary trained on the project's own corpus. This is near-free in Rust.
- **New information to the receiver:** C(message | receiver's context) = C(context + message) − C(context). This is the compression-based conditional complexity behind normalized compression distance (Cilibrasi & Vitányi).
- **Redundancy** = 1 − C(msg | ctx) / C(msg).
- It reveals when a brief pastes context the receiver already has (a direct sustainability lever) and when a handback carries almost nothing new.
- This is the counting argument from the imbrication study turned on ourselves: what a message costs is what it adds beyond what the receiver already holds.

**2. Where each agent stands, read from its language:**
- **Interpretable anchor.** Represent each agent per wave as a distribution over the framing doc's vocabulary: the symbols and named objects (imbrex, c(G), κ, scrupulus…). Back it with a small local embedding model for meaning beyond exact terms; all-MiniLM is already in the HF cache, and it runs on CPU.
- **Map of the team.** Jensen–Shannon divergence between agents' distributions, laid out in 2D per wave, shows who is near whom and how that moves over waves.
- **Who owns what.** Mutual information between agent identity and terms shows which concepts are distinctive of which agent, so you can see the problem being divided up, or not.
- **Drift from the question.** Divergence between the wave notes and `framing.md §0`, your own words, gives you a direct view of the "answering a reformulation" failure.
- **Pair independence.** Compare the verifier's independent first entry in `__examen__` with the author's claim. If the verifier's language converges on the author's before it has produced its own result, that is a measurable signature of the agreement cascade.
- **New puzzles.** The distance of each scrupulus from existing claims separates real anomalies from restatements.

**3. Semantic entropy** (Kuhn et al.; Farquhar et al., *Nature* 2024: sample several answers, cluster them by mutual entailment, take the entropy over the clusters).
- The textbook version costs N extra generations per question, which is too expensive per message.
- The design gives a version almost for free. When author and verifier, or parallel explorers, independently state a result, the semantic entropy across those *independent* statements measures how unsettled the claim is, with no extra sampling.
- Reserve the full sampled version for disputed claims and for claims at synthesis.

**The guard: these are instruments for attention, not targets.**
- Measure silently. Agents are never told they are scored on entropy or divergence; if they were, they would optimise the measure (Goodhart).
- Nothing gates on these numbers. They appear as one or two lines in the brief, e.g. "explorer B has drifted from your question; verifier V adopted the author's vocabulary before its independent result". The PI and you decide what to make of them, consistent with the v2 correction.
- Words are not positions. Two agents can share terms and mean different things, which is why the embedding sits beside the vocabulary.
- I quoted the references above from memory and would verify them before they go into the design.

**Where it lives in v2:**
- `libripens hook subagent-stop` adds a `comm` event to `__expensa__`: from, to, kind, tokens, compressed bits, new bits given receiver, redundancy. Communication is a spend, so it belongs in the ledger.
- `libripens map --wave` is an offline subcommand: embeddings plus divergences, output as a 2D map and a short table of anomalies. Embedding on CPU is cheap, but it is still off the hot path.
- Semantic entropy is computed only on demand for disputed or synthesis-bound claims.
- The brief gains one line of position signals, after the scrupuli and before spend.
- The benchmark survey's "exploration diversity" metric (embedding variance of probes) becomes one output of the same map.

1. **`UserPromptSubmit` captures your words automatically.** Every genuine prompt you send in a lab session is appended verbatim to the user-words channel. You no longer need to remember `/lab-steer`, and no agent ever writes your words. Subagent hand-backs and cross-session messages, which also fire this event, are logged separately as communication events.
2. **`SubagentStart` injects the per-run context.** Wave, claim id, partner agent and the honesty contract reach every subagent through `additionalContext`. umbod's "the contract travels with delegation" becomes guaranteed, and the PI stops pasting boilerplate into briefs, which saves communication.
3. **`PostToolUse` on `SendMessage` mirrors pair conversations into `__examen__`.** Mirroring no longer depends on the agents remembering to do it. The same hook is where each message gets its information measures: bits, new bits for the receiver, redundancy.
4. **`watchPaths` and `FileChanged` make the back-flow live.** When a verifier raises a scrupulus or a claim becomes disputed, a one-line notice reaches the PI and you immediately, not at the next session brief.
5. **`PreCompact` and `PostCompact` measure the PI's own attention.** The compaction summary is stored, and the measure is which open scrupuli the PI's context dropped when it was compressed. That is v2's root cause, now observable.
6. **`mcp_tool` handlers.** Hooks call `libripens` as a resident MCP server instead of starting a process per event. Combined with `async` for anything heavier than appending a line, the hooks stay off the critical path.

A few smaller ones are also worth having:
- `MessageDisplay` can show claim ids with their *current* label as you read, while the transcript stays unchanged.
- `PreModelSwitch` warns you of the cache-rewrite cost in dollars before a model switch.
- `InstructionsLoaded` hashes the instruction files to check prompt-cache stability.
- `SessionEnd` writes the closing Wh and tokens per accepted claim. It has a 1.5 s budget, one more argument for Rust.
- `TeammateIdle` keeps a verifier working until its thread has a verdict, if we fall back to Agent Teams.

One deliberate exclusion: the LLM-evaluated `prompt` and `agent` handlers are off by default. They would put judgement into hooks and cost tokens on every event. They converge independently on the same flaw, and they're right. The wave-1 finding should have made me cut, not only rename. I accept the verdict.

**Which test, and how.** I'd run them in sequence:
1. Fable's one-day test as a cheap screen.
2. Opus's controlled test only if the screen says go, as the real validation before building `libripens`.

Opus also spotted a contamination problem the screen must avoid: our design documents name the five signals it would score. So the replay has to run in a copy of the genesis repo pinned before the decision point, with no access to Murmuration or the retrospectives. A separate agent should score it without knowing which arm produced which run.

**One principle question is yours.** The follow-or-park rule is a gate on the PI, which v2 ruled out. My view is that it is a different kind of rule:
- It doesn't tell the PI *what* to decide or *when*; parking with a reason is always allowed.
- It only forbids leaving a puzzle silently unhandled, which is exactly how the genesis signals were lost.

That makes it accountability, not direction. Running it as arm C lets evidence settle whether it helps.

If you agree, wave 2 becomes this screen rather than the build. Here is what I would freeze until the screen says go:
- `libripens` in Rust;
- the 25-hook set;
- the SQLite index;
- most instruments.

The hardening skill and the agent files stay; both reviewers say they survive either way.

You're right on both counts, and the second one changes the evaluation question entirely. Once Murmuration runs on itself, its own transcripts become the test data. That replaces statistical power we can't afford with use, plus your judgement on what it proposes. So the design only has to be good enough to produce honest, inspectable runs. It doesn't need to be instrumented for universality.

**What genesis says actually helped the agents** (evidence, not design):

| Helped | How it worked in genesis | Needs a hook? |
|:--|:--|:--|
| One framing and notation document | Agents read it first; almost no drift in symbols | No |
| A brief template: read-first list, the question in the user's words, rules, an uncapped "what puzzled you" section | Wave 1 produced its best signals exactly when asked this way | No |
| Claim labels, with the latest verdict overriding | Reviews argued about labels, not prose; nothing overclaimed reached the notebook | No |
| Independent verifiers (reproducer, proof adversary) that record their own result first | Caught every real error | No |
| Warm agents for corrections, fresh agents for checks | Cheap fixes, independent checks | No |
| Files others can find: reports, claims, puzzles, plus colgrep | Agents pulled sections instead of rereading | No |

**What failed and needs something structural:**
1. **Your words drifted out of the PI's notes.** "Combinatorics" never appeared in them.
2. **Signals reached the PI and weren't taken up.**
3. **The PI's own claims were never checked.**
4. **One agent killed another agent's job.**

Of these, only the first is worth a hook. The second and third are fixed by the PI's own documents: a wave note that ends with each open puzzle marked *followed* or *parked, because…*, and the PI's factual claims filed like any worker claim. The fourth is a permission deny rule (`Bash(pkill:*)`, `Bash(killall:*)`) in settings, not a hook.

**So the minimal lab is:**
- **Agents:** research-pi (Opus, prose identity); explorer and author (Sonnet); reproducer and proof-adversary (Sonnet).
- **One skill,** `research-loop`, containing:
  - the brief template;
  - the labels;
  - the wave-note template with puzzle dispositions;
  - the default-prompt blocks the `agent` setting drops.
- **Stores as plain markdown, one file per writer.** No Rust, no SQLite, no MCP server: everything stays readable, diffable and colgrep-searchable.
  - `__pondus__/<claim>.md`: verifiers append their verdict sections.
  - `__scrupuli__/<wave>-<agent>.md`.
  - `__statera__/<wave>.md`.
- **Two hooks, both on rare events:**
  - `UserPromptSubmit` appends your genuine prompts verbatim to the user-words file;
  - `SessionStart(resume|compact)` re-shows the current wave note and open puzzles after context loss.
- **A small `lab status` script,** run on demand: open puzzles, disputed claims, and spend read from Claude Code's own transcripts. That replaces the ledger hook; the transcripts already record every token.
- **No live instruments.** Measurement moves to the reflective run, offline, over transcripts.

**The reflective run, in short:**
- **Question:** "how should Murmuration change?"
- **Data:** the transcripts and stores of earlier runs, starting with the genesis study.
- **Who does what:** explorers read the logs; authors propose changes as claims; verifiers check those claims against the transcripts.
- **Guardrail:** changes to agent files and skills always come to you as proposals, never silent self-edits.

**What I'd freeze, not delete:** v5's `libripens`, the 25-hook set, the SQLite index and the instruments stay documented. Any of them comes back only if a reflective run shows a concrete need.
